title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
The failure here is a model asserting nonexistent legal authorities as fact. An AI tool called Irys generated fabricated case citations, invented case titles, and false quotations, which the lawyer then submitted across multiple court filings without verifying that the cited cases existed. The error entered the deployment at the point where a human was expected to check the tool's output against real legal sources, and that check did not happen because the lawyer mistakenly believed Irys was connected to a verified legal research subscription.

This is a well-documented failure mode for large language models used in legal drafting: the model produces plausible-looking citations that have no counterpart in actual case law. Catching it would have required the attorney to independently verify each citation in a confirmed legal database before filing. The gap between what the tool actually did and what the user believed it was doing, namely drawing from a trusted subscription service, was the proximate condition that allowed the fabrications to reach a court.

What is not established is whether any sanction, adverse ruling, or finding of bad faith has been issued against the lawyers or the firm, and the reported figures on industry-wide AI adoption and hallucination counts are drawn from third-party tracking rather than verified by any adjudicatory body.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized after their legal filings in a Los Angeles lawsuit contained artificially generated fake cases, nonexistent quotes, and invented legal holdings. The lawsuit was filed by homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga in July 2024 against State Farm and others following a 2020 fire that damaged her Carson home. After a contractor began repairs, a storm caused additional water damage, and delays in getting State Farm's approval prevented the work from being completed. Meni-Siliga and her husband exhausted their savings and retirement accounts, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys to prepare some motions and confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and quotes. She mistakenly believed Irys was connected to her firm's legal research subscription. The case is scheduled for trial in October. This incident highlights a growing problem in the legal industry, where 41 percent of law firms use generative AI, and a database tracked 1,922 documented legal hallucination cases worldwide, mostly in the United States.
